title: Chapter XXII
paragraphs: Summer ended, followed by early autumn. Michaelmas had passed, but the harvest was late that year and a few fields still stood uncut. Mr. Linton and his daughter often walked out among the reapers. When the last sheaves were being brought in, they stayed until dusk. The evening was cold and damp, and my master caught a bad cold that settled stubbornly on his lungs and kept him indoors almost continuously throughout the winter.

Poor Cathy, frightened into giving up her little romance, had been much sadder and quieter since it ended. Her father insisted that she read less and exercise more. Since he could no longer walk with her, I felt it my duty to replace his company with mine as far as possible. I was a poor substitute: with all my daily work, I could spare only two or three hours to accompany her, and she clearly preferred his company to mine.

One afternoon in October or early November, I asked her to give up her walk because I was certain it would rain. It was a cool, watery afternoon; wet, dead leaves rustled over the grass and paths, and dark grey streaks of cloud were racing up from the west, half covering the cold blue sky and promising heavy rain. She refused, so I reluctantly put on a cloak, took my umbrella, and went with her towards the lower end of the park. She usually chose that orderly path when she was low in spirits, as she always was when Mr. Edgar was worse than usual. He never admitted it, but she and I guessed from his increased silence and the sadness of his face. She walked sorrowfully, without running or skipping, though the cold wind might well have encouraged a race. Often, out of the corner of my eye, I saw her raise a hand and brush something from her cheek. I looked about for a way to distract her. Beside the road rose a steep, rough bank where hazels and stunted oaks clung precariously, their roots half exposed. The soil was too loose for the oaks, and strong winds had pushed some almost horizontal. In summer Miss Catherine loved climbing along their trunks and sitting in the branches, swinging twenty feet above the ground. Delighted as I was by her nimbleness and carefree childish heart, I still thought it proper to scold whenever I found her so high up—but in a way that told her she needn’t come down. Between dinner and tea she would lie in her cradle rocked by the breeze, singing old songs I had taught her in the nursery, or watching the birds who shared it feed their young and coax them into flight. Or she would nestle there with her eyes shut, half thinking, half dreaming, happier than words could express.

“Look, Miss!” I cried, pointing beneath the roots of a twisted tree. “Winter hasn’t arrived yet. There’s a little flower up there, the last bloom of all those bluebells that covered the grassy steps with a lilac mist in July. Will you climb up and pick it for papa?”
Cathy gazed for a long time at the lonely flower trembling in its little shelter of earth. At last she said, “No, I won’t touch it. But it looks sad, doesn’t it, Ellen?”
“Yes,” I remarked, “about as chilled and drooping as you. There’s no colour in your cheeks. Let’s hold hands and run. You’re so listless, I daresay I’ll keep up.”

“No,” she repeated, and kept walking slowly. Now and then she stopped to contemplate some moss, a tuft of faded grass, or a bright orange fungus spreading among heaps of brown leaves. Every so often her hand went up to her turned-away face.
“Catherine, why are you crying, love?” I asked, coming close and putting my arm round her shoulders. “You mustn’t cry because papa has a cold. Be thankful it’s nothing worse.”
Now she stopped trying to control her tears. Sobs choked her breath.

“Oh, it _will_ become something worse,” she said. “What will I do when papa and you leave me and I’m all alone? I can’t forget what you said, Ellen. I hear it all the time. How different life will be, how dreary the world, when you and papa are dead.”

“Nobody knows whether you might die before us,” I replied. “It’s wrong to expect trouble in advance. Let’s hope we all have years and years ahead. Your father is young, and I’m strong and barely forty-five. My mother lived to eighty and was a lively woman to the end. Suppose Mr. Linton lives to sixty: that would leave him more years than you’ve lived yourself, Miss. Wouldn’t it be foolish to mourn a disaster more than twenty years before it happens?”
“But Aunt Isabella was younger than papa,” she said, looking up with timid hope for further comfort.

“Aunt Isabella didn’t have you and me to nurse her,” I replied. “She wasn’t as happy as your father and had less to live for. All you need to do is care for him properly, cheer him by being cheerful yourself, and avoid giving him anything to worry about. Remember that, Cathy! I won’t hide it from you: you might kill him if you behaved wildly and recklessly, nursing some foolish romantic fancy for the son of a man who’d be glad to see him in his grave, and let him discover that you were grieving over the separation he thought necessary.”

“Nothing in the world worries me except papa’s illness,” she answered. “Nothing matters beside papa. And I’ll never—never—oh, never, as long as I have my senses, do or say anything to upset him. I love him more than myself, Ellen, and this is how I know: every night I pray to outlive him, because I’d rather suffer than have him suffer. That proves I love him more than myself.”
“Fine words,” I replied. “But your actions must prove it too. When he’s well again, don’t forget the promises you made while you were afraid.”

As we talked, we approached a door in the wall opening on to the road. My young lady’s spirits brightened again. She climbed up and sat on the wall, reaching for scarlet rosehips on the highest branches of the wild roses overhanging the roadside. All the lower fruit had gone; only birds could reach what was left unless they sat where Cathy was. As she stretched for them, her hat fell off. Since the door was locked, she proposed climbing down to fetch it. I warned her not to fall, and she nimbly disappeared. Getting back was another matter. The stones were smooth and neatly mortared, and neither the roses nor the trailing brambles could help her climb. Foolishly, I didn’t remember this until I heard her laughing and calling, “Ellen! You’ll have to fetch the key, or I’ll have to run round to the lodge. I can’t scale the battlements from this side!”
“Stay there,” I answered. “I’ve got my keys in my pocket. Perhaps one will open it. If not, I’ll go.”

Catherine amused herself by dancing back and forth outside the door while I tried the larger keys one after another. The last failed like the rest. I told her again to stay where she was and was about to hurry home as fast as possible when an approaching sound stopped me: a horse trotting. Cathy stopped dancing too.
“Who is it?” I whispered.
“Ellen, I wish you could open the door,” she whispered back anxiously.
“Hello, Miss Linton!” the rider’s deep voice called. “I’m glad I’ve met you. Don’t hurry inside. I want an explanation from you, and I mean to have it.”
“I won’t speak to you, Mr. Heathcliff,” Catherine answered. “Papa says you’re a wicked man and you hate us both. Ellen says so too.”

“That’s beside the point,” Heathcliff said—for it was he. “I don’t hate my son, presumably, and it’s about him that you must listen. Yes, you’ve reason to blush. Two or three months ago you were writing to Linton, weren’t you? Playing at love, eh? You both deserved a whipping for that! Especially you, being older and, as it turns out, less sensitive. I have your letters, and if you’re impertinent I’ll send them to your father. I suppose you grew bored with the amusement and gave it up? Well, when you dropped it, you dropped Linton into a Slough of Despond. He was serious, truly in love. As surely as I live, he’s dying for you, his heart breaking because you’ve changed. Not in a manner of speaking: actually breaking. Hareton has mocked him constantly for six weeks, and I’ve tried stronger measures, trying to frighten him out of his foolishness. But he grows worse every day. Unless you bring him back to life, he’ll be in his grave before summer!”

“How can you tell that poor child such blatant lies?” I called from inside the wall. “Please ride on! How can you deliberately invent such contemptible falsehoods? Miss Cathy, I’ll break the lock with a stone. Don’t believe that vile nonsense. Your own heart can tell you that nobody could die of love for a stranger.”

“I didn’t realise anyone was listening,” the exposed villain muttered. Then, louder: “Worthy Mrs. Dean, I like you, but I don’t like your deceit. How could _you_ tell such blatant lies as to say I hated the ‘poor child’, and invent bogey stories to frighten her away from my doorstep? Catherine Linton—the very name warms my heart—my bonny lass, I’ll be away all week. Go and see whether I’ve told the truth. Do, there’s a darling! Imagine your father in my place and Linton in yours. What would you think of your careless lover if he wouldn’t take a single step to comfort you, even when your father himself begged him? Don’t be stupid enough to make the same mistake. I swear by my salvation that he’s going to his grave, and only you can save him!”
The lock broke, and I came out.

“I swear Linton is dying,” Heathcliff repeated, staring hard at me. “Grief and disappointment are hurrying his death. Nelly, if you won’t let her go, you can walk over yourself. But I won’t be back until this time next week, and I scarcely think even your master would object to her visiting her cousin.”
“Come inside,” I said, taking Cathy by the arm and half forcing her through the door. She lingered, looking anxiously at his face, whose sternness gave away none of the deception beneath.
He urged his horse closer, bent down, and said:

“Miss Catherine, I’ll admit I have little patience with Linton, and Hareton and Joseph have less. I’ll admit he’s among harsh people. He longs for kindness as well as love, and a kind word from you would be his best medicine. Ignore Mrs. Dean’s cruel warnings. Be generous and find a way to see him. He dreams of you night and day, and because you neither visit nor write, nothing can persuade him that you don’t hate him.”

I shut the door and rolled a stone against it to help the damaged lock hold. Opening my umbrella, I drew Cathy beneath it. Rain was beginning to drive through the moaning branches, warning us to hurry. We said nothing of Heathcliff as we hastened home, but I instinctively knew that a double darkness now weighed on Catherine’s heart. Her face was so sad it scarcely looked like hers. Plainly she believed every word he had said.

The master had gone to bed before we returned. Cathy slipped into his room to ask how he was, but he was asleep. She came back and asked me to sit with her in the library. We had tea together. Afterwards she lay on the rug and asked me not to talk, saying she was tired. I took a book and pretended to read. Once she thought I was absorbed, she began silently crying again; it seemed to be her favourite occupation just then. I let her indulge it for a while, then protested, mocking and ridiculing everything Mr. Heathcliff had said about his son as though I were sure she would agree. Alas! I had no skill to undo the effect of his story. It had worked exactly as he intended.
“You may be right, Ellen,” she answered, “but I won’t have any peace until I know. And I must tell Linton it isn’t my fault I don’t write, and make him understand I won’t change.”

What good were anger and protests against her foolish willingness to believe him? We parted that night on hostile terms. Yet next day I was on the road to Wuthering Heights beside my wilful young mistress’s pony. I couldn’t bear her grief, her pale, dejected face and heavy eyes. I gave in, faintly hoping that Linton’s own welcome would show how little truth there was in the story.
